summary: This Poison Control article on tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia) explains its long use as a natural remedy, mainly for skin conditions, and the evidence behind those uses. It stresses that tea tree oil is poisonous if swallowed and should not be used in or around the mouth, and it covers side effects, pet poisonings, household use, and two real poisoning cases.
one_line: Poison Control's overview of tea tree oil: skin-remedy evidence, the danger of swallowing it, pet toxicity, and real poisoning cases.
key_facts: Tea tree oil comes from the leaves of an Australian tree called Melaleuca alternifolia.
In 2011, Poison Control received nearly twice as many calls about tea tree oil than any other named essential oil, including cinnamon oil, clove oil, and eucalyptus oil.
More than 10 percent of people exposed to tea tree oil were treated in a hospital or doctor's office.
The National Library of Medicine (NLM) notes that its traditional uses of tea tree oil have not all been tested for safety or effectiveness.
A 1994 study found tea tree oil and the antifungal drug clotrimazole had approximately the same effect in treating fingernail fungus.
A 1990 study found that tea tree oil and benzoyl peroxide were both effective against acne, but tea tree oil took longer to work and had fewer side effects.
A 1992 study found tea tree oil was no better than a placebo in curing fungus infection, though it improved symptoms as much as tolnaftate.
A single report described breast enlargement in a young boy who used products containing lavender oil and tea tree oil.
A child who swallowed a small amount of tea tree oil given to him by mistake went into a coma from which he recovered.

Veterinary toxicologists reported that large amounts of tea tree oil applied to the skin of cats and dogs caused poisoning, with symptoms including muscle tremors, weakness, difficulty in walking, low body temperature, and excessive salivation.
The article warns that swallowed tea tree oil can cause dangerous poisoning in less than thirty minutes.
Poison Control advises that tea tree oil should NOT be taken by mouth for any reason, even though some traditional uses include mouthwash, bad breath, toothache and mouth ulcers.
In Case 1, an elderly male who swallowed a teaspoon of tea tree oil recovered after dizziness, vomiting and slurred speech, and his EKG and vital signs were normal.
In Case 2, a middle-aged woman used tea tree oil and 3% hydrogen peroxide as an enema and presented with bloody diarrhea, requiring intravenous fluids and pain medication.
The article's medical reviewer is Rose Ann Gould Soloway, RN, BSN, MSEd, DABAT emerita, Clinical Toxicologist.
